title: Becoming Indispensable at a New Job
body: This is the framework I'd run starting any admin or coordination-heavy role. Not a slow ramp-up. A deliberate push to become hard to replace in the first few weeks.

Join an AI notetaker to every meeting, since nobody likes training you on the same thing twice. When something is ambiguous, ask directly how you'll know if you did a good job, what good actually looks like. In spare moments, work a chatbot for context on the industry and, where you can get it connected, the internal processes too. Spend real time understanding the structure of everything around you. That's what makes humans valuable and what makes you effective at delegating to AI in the first place. Push to get AI connected into every system you touch. Have it read meeting transcripts and start handling the work that's obvious from them. Then keep taking on more.

This works because so much of admin work is coordination and process knowledge, exactly what AI is good at once someone points it in the right direction. The person who does this in their first month looks like a completely different hire than the one who waits to be told what to do.

title: Do You Know How to Delegate?
body: The best mental model I've found for delegating to AI: imagine a smart kid just walked in to help you. They can write, research, work a spreadsheet, whatever you need. But they know nothing about your company, your situation, or what "good" looks like for you.
You can outsource your thinking to them. You can't outsource your understanding. If you don't know what a good result looks like yourself, no amount of prompting fixes that.
Build the understanding first. Then delegate.

title: The Intern Test
body: If you wouldn't let a new, keen intern do the task, don't rely on AI to do it.

Don't use AI to respond to a frustrated customer. Do use AI to sort and route the incoming tickets. Don't use AI to write the proposal for your most important deal. Do use AI to draft the first version from a standard template. Don't use AI to decide which opportunities to prioritize. Do use AI to pull the data so you can make that call yourself.
The intern isn't the limitation. The intern is the standard. If you'd trust someone new, with good instructions and some oversight, AI can handle it. If you wouldn't, keep your hands on it.

title: Accomplishments, Not Goals
body: Vague goals don't fail loudly. They just quietly never happen. So I changed how I set them.

Before I plan what I'm going to do, I write what I want to be able to say I did. Not goals. Accomplishments. Goals are forward-looking and vague. Accomplishments are past-tense and specific. "Grow the business" is a goal. "Closed our first enterprise customer" is an accomplishment.
Once I have the list, the work becomes obvious. I'm not deciding what to prioritize, I'm reverse-engineering what has to happen for each of those stories to be real.

The uncomfortable part: you have to commit to a story before you know if it's achievable. I've had years where December arrived and I hadn't done what I wrote. But I still got closer than I would have.

title: Trust Is an Incentive, Not a Feeling
body: You can't verify what a company does with your data. You can't audit their servers. You can't read their internal policies. You have to trust something. What I trust is incentives.

If a company's business model depends on customers continuing to use and pay for their product, breaking that trust is supposed to be expensive. Except sometimes it isn't. Facebook's user base grew 13% the year after Cambridge Analytica. Revenue went up 49%. The stock fully recovered.

Turns out the incentive only bites when leaving is actually an option. Nobody quit Facebook over data misuse because quitting meant losing every conversation, every photo, every person you'd have to re-find on some other app. The exit cost more than the betrayal did.

For most of the software you actually choose between, switching costs an afternoon, not your identity. That's exactly when incentives start doing real work. Not blind trust. Not naive trust either. Trust that only means something when you could walk away and the company knows it.

title: The Cost of Context
body: Dumb AI and smart AI use the same model. The difference is context.

For a long time I wondered why my AI outputs felt generic. Then I realized I was giving it generic inputs. Not because I meant to. Because I hadn't built the structure to give it the right context automatically.

Now I have a memory system. Files that tell the AI who I am, what I'm working on, what good looks like for me, what I care about and what I don't. Every prompt loads the right context without me having to re-explain myself.
The difference between an AI that feels like a tool and one that feels like a collaborator is almost always this. Not the model. The context.

title: Run on Signals of Imbalance
body: What's actually the bottleneck? It depends on where things are really waiting. If the customer is waiting, that's an operational bottleneck. If operations can clearly handle more, maybe the constraint is sales. And if the business is pointed in the wrong direction entirely, it doesn't matter how hard any one team is working. You can't rerun the business under a different decision to find out, so effort alone can't tell you where the real constraint is.

What can tell you is imbalance. It works like inventory: too low and things break, too high and finance gets upset. Either extreme produces its own kind of friction, and that friction is the signal. The goal is building systems that amplify the under-represented signal instead of letting it go unnoticed until it's a crisis.

This is where AI agents earn their keep. Have one research the biggest risks to an idea ahead of time and pre-plan the pivot for each one. Once you already know what you'd do if a given risk hit, that risk stops being nearly as risky, and that's what actually opens room for bigger bets. Visibility into your real constraints, not just faster execution, is one of the biggest levers in a business.

title: Naming Your Days
body: Before the week starts, I name a main focus for each day. That way nothing important gets neglected just because it wasn't the loudest thing that day. A big project can get two full focus days while two or three other priorities still get real attention across the rest of the week.

It's basically production scheduling applied to your own time. Lock in the near-term schedule, then treat that lock-in as real. Some cleanup and reactive work will always bleed into a focus day, and true emergencies get to bump the plan.

The part that matters is the bar for what counts as a bump. If things that aren't actually emergencies keep knocking your top projects off the schedule, you're not planning your time anymore, you're just running a reactive department. Protecting the lock-in is what keeps you steering instead of getting steered.

title: Long Focus Blocks Are Getting Scarce
body: For small tasks, a 15-minute timer works great. Decide what you're going to do with the 15 minutes, commit to finishing it in that window, and you knock it out.

That method falls apart for real deep work. I recently spent three hours on one task, start to finish, no restarts. It felt different than usual, mostly because it's rare now. I'm convinced I was more effective working it straight through than I would have been picking it up and putting it down five separate times.

AI makes this harder to protect. Jumping between AI tools and tasks all day is genuinely useful for a lot of work, but some work still needs a long, uninterrupted block of human focus, and that kind of block is exactly what a day full of quick AI exchanges tends to erode.

title: Auto-Publishing to My Website
body: I just set things up so I can talk into a custom GPT and publish a note directly to my website. An idea can now go from something I'm thinking about to something published here with almost no friction.

This note itself is the first real test. I'm talking through the idea, turning it into a note, and sending it to the site through the same workflow I want to use going forward. I'm excited to see it actually work.

The easier I make the pathway from having an idea to publishing it, the more likely I am to share the small thoughts and lessons that would otherwise never make it out of my head. I'm excited to see what I can share and how useful I can make this website over time.

title: Are You the Adult or the Child?
body: These are two roles we alternate through life, and sometimes take both nearly simultaneously.
I don't mean these in the traditional sense. This has nothing to do with age, it's about a maturity continuum.
I call someone a child when they're impacted by circumstances of any scale. I call someone an adult when they're responsible for having impact on another person.
A child is excited about their upcoming birthday party. An adult makes the cake. A child has a bad day. An adult pushes through and fakes a smile so the child doesn't worry.
Taking either role isn't good or bad, it's a matter of judgment in the moment.
A mistake adults make far too often is feeling pressured into the adult role when we're actually the one in need of care, when it would serve us better to admit to struggle and let someone help.

The other extreme doesn't work either. Are you a special person? Do you think the bad circumstances you're in are someone else's responsibility, and that others are obligated to accommodate you? Maybe you need to grow up.
A mature person develops an objective view of reality and switches roles as needed. Reality is hard, but it gets easier through acceptance and understanding.

We all have needs. Circumstances impact all of us. How we react to circumstances can have a massive impact on future circumstances, even though a lot is outside our control. Every person is deeply responsible for the life experience of their neighbor, choosing not to interact with a neighbor is still a choice, the same as choosing to destroy them or invest everything in seeing them prosper.

You can't pick up one end of a stick. You get the whole thing, no matter what. One-ended sticks don't exist. Choosing the role of the child forces the other party into the role of the adult. When someone is able to be the adult, giving them that opportunity can be a gift, the opportunity to serve and care for others is the only true meaning in life.
Healthy adult-to-adult relationships involve regular role-swapping, with both parties aware of each other's needs and capabilities. A dual-child relationship will always escalate.
Every external need you've ever had has cost someone else in a way you'll never fully know, especially since successful care is, by definition, invisible.

list: Be unreasonably grateful for the adults in your life.
Let others have the privilege of giving to you. Be a good receiver, respond with gratitude rather than refusing help.
Get comfortable being uncomfortable. That's how you develop your "adulting" capacity.

body: So, are you the adult, or the child?

title: List of Questions to Increase Your Productivity

list: Identify your current main objectives in life / high-level goals.
What are your top ten productivity killers?
Identify the top three killers you have the most influence over.
Brainstorm how to solve the top three killers.
Identify the top action you can take in the next day to improve your productivity.
What is the top thing you "should be doing" but keep putting off?
Commit to having a better day tomorrow, and work on the top three items for the next week.
Clarify when you want to be productive and when you want to be down (just a general outline).
You can drastically impact your productivity by being in proximity to a high performer.
Accountability: sending 15-minute time sheets to another person is a massive productivity hack.

The Pomodoro technique has a major flaw. If you're still productively working after 25 minutes, don't stop. Breaking while you're in a flow state is simply an interruption. Don't stop a roller coaster for a snack break.

title: Organizing Stuff
body: Our brains get bogged down if we try to do more than one thing at a time. If you want to clean up a space, here's a step-by-step guide so you don't get overwhelmed.

list: Open space for sorting required.
Garbage can.
Vacuum cleaner.
Limit the project size to what you're confident you can finish.
Take everything into your sorting space.
If your sorting space is limited, pick a specific section to work on.
Discard everything that's obvious garbage.
Clean the area that is now empty.
Decide what categorizations make the most sense.

sublist: Should probably discard but don't want to
Tools, anything you'll want to find when a need arises. Example: misc cables.

list: Put everything away.
Sets must stay together, think of them as one item when organizing.

title: What AI Can Never Do For You
body: Knowing what to ask in the first place, and holding the focus to actually act on the answer once you have it.
It can draft the email, build the report, run the analysis. But when it's wrong, the responsibility doesn't land on the AI. It lands on whoever hit send.
The value was never really the advice. AI gives good advice constantly, it's not scarce anymore. What's still scarce is two things it can never do for you.
Focus and responsibility were never the parts of the job that AI was going to take. They were the job.

title: AI Is Not the Great Equalizer
body: The common narrative is that AI levels the playing field, same tools, same access, equal footing for everyone. It's not true, and I'd argue it does the opposite.

Your understanding and your AI ability aren't additive, they're closer to a multiplier. [Terence Tao got real mathematical insight out of ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/6a5fdc7a-d6f8-83e8-bbea-8deb42cfed56) in under three minutes on a question most people couldn't even ask. That's basically [Jim Yagmin's point](https://yagmin.com/blog/code-is-the-byproduct/) too: the output is just the byproduct of understanding, not the goal itself.

So the people who use AI to learn something new every single day aren't getting ahead a little. They're compounding an advantage daily, against people using the same AI to avoid learning at all. That gap isn't fair, and it isn't going to close. It's going to get very visible, very fast.

title: AI Had Access to Everything, It Still Analyzed Almost Nothing
body: I asked AI to deeply analyze a large connected dataset. Every source was plugged in, full access, on paper. It could see everything, in theory.

It handed back an analysis built on a tiny slice of what was actually available. Maybe the model got lazy. Maybe it just did exactly what it was told with exactly what it had. From the outside, those look identical.

I only caught it because I knew what was happening in the background. Most people wouldn't. Being wired up to a data source doesn't mean that data actually reaches the context window where the model reasons. If it never gets pulled in, it's invisible, no matter how many integrations you've got.
You don't have to know how the model reasons. You do have to know what it's actually working with. Otherwise you're trusting output that was built on input you never checked.

title: Your Entire Life Is Made Up of Loops
body: Your entire life is made up of loops. Trigger, behavior, reward, repeat. Every habit you have, good or bad, is running on the same basic mechanism.

The loop isn't the problem. The trajectory is. Stress that leads to scrolling gives you the same immediate relief as stress that leads to exercise. Run either one for a year and you end up in completely different places.
That's the trap with a destructive habit. It isn't failing, it's succeeding, just at the wrong thing. A loop can feel like it's working today and still be wrecking you over time.

You can't fix that by deciding to be a different person. Identity doesn't lead, it follows. Change what you actually do, on repeat, and give it long enough. Every loop has a trajectory. Change loops, change trajectory.

title: Playing Monopoly in Real Life
body: Monopoly is a useful model for thinking about risk and opportunity. Buying properties creates luck surface area: the more properties you own, the more chances you have to get paid. In real life, those “properties” might be businesses, investments, skills, relationships, products, or actual real estate. Once something shows potential, adding houses is the equivalent of putting more resources behind it—hiring employees, investing more capital, expanding a business, or developing property.

But you need enough cash to survive bad rolls. If everything is invested when an unexpected expense arrives, you can be forced to sell assets at a loss or take on expensive debt. At the same time, too much cash eventually becomes a disadvantage. Once you have enough liquidity to survive reasonable losses, additional idle cash provides less protection and could instead be producing income or increasing your exposure to upside.

This works best when investments are somewhat reversible. If I put $100,000 into something that could reasonably be sold for $80,000, my downside isn’t necessarily the entire $100,000. I can deploy capital while retaining an escape route. Real life is harder than Monopoly, though, because assets aren’t guaranteed to sell when I need them. My safety shouldn’t be based on total net worth, but on how much liquidity I could actually access during bad conditions.

The strategy is simple: create opportunities, keep enough cash to survive, develop the promising opportunities, and recycle the profits into more opportunities. The goal isn’t to avoid bad rolls. It’s to build a position where bad rolls are survivable and good rolls are increasingly valuable.
